title: The Preprocessor
relevance: Interviewers probe whether candidates understand that the preprocessor is dumb text substitution—explaining #include, macro pitfalls, include guards/ODR, and why modern C++ prefers constexpr/inline over macros.

phases.goal: Establish that the preprocessor runs before compilation as pure text substitution and how #include and #define work.

must_hit.point: The preprocessor does not understand C++ syntax; it performs pure text substitution on the source before compilation begins.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says the preprocessor manipulates source text and runs before the compiler translates to machine instructions.

must_hit.point: #include literally copy-pastes another file's contents at the directive; angle brackets search system include paths, quotes search the local directory first then system paths.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts #include <...> (system paths) vs #include "..." (local first, then system).

must_hit.point: #define creates a macro that replaces subsequent occurrences of an identifier with replacement text; #undef removes a macro definition.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes object-like macros as simple replacements and notes #undef clears the definition.

must_hit.point: Function-like macros take arguments that the preprocessor substitutes into the replacement text without evaluating them first.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions argument substitution into the body with no prior evaluation, e.g. MIN-style macros.

probes: What does the preprocessor do, and how does #include differ between angle brackets and quotes?

hints.1: Think about what happens to your source file before the compiler proper runs.
hints.2: Cover text substitution, #include search rules, and what #define/#undef do.
hints.3: Preprocessor: pure text sub before compile; #include pastes files (<> system, "" local then system); #define replaces identifiers, #undef removes them.

phases.goal: Explain macro pitfalls, conditional compilation, include guards, predefined macros, and # / ## operators.

must_hit.point: Function-like macros need parentheses around every parameter and the whole body to avoid operator-precedence bugs when complex expressions are passed.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Cites BAD_SQ(x) x * x vs SQ(x) ((x)*(x)), and that BAD_SQ(i+1) can expand with wrong precedence.

must_hit.point: If a macro argument has side effects (e.g. i++), it can be evaluated multiple times, which can cause undefined behaviour.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains SQ(i++) expanding to ((i++)*(i++)) with double increment / UB.

must_hit.point: Conditional compilation (#ifdef/#ifndef/#if/#elif/#else/#endif) includes or excludes code based on whether macros are defined or what values they hold.
Include guards (#ifndef/#define/#endif) or #pragma once ensure a header's contents are processed only once when headers include other headers.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says multiple inclusion can cause multiple definitions of the same class/struct; guards or #pragma once prevent that.

must_hit.point: The stringise operator (#) turns a macro argument into a string literal; the token-paste operator (##) concatenates two tokens into one.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives PRINT_VAR_NAME(var) with #var and MAKE_VAR(name,num) with name##num.

must_hit.point: __FILE__, __LINE__, __DATE__, and __TIME__ are predefined object-like macros; __func__ is a compiler-provided implicitly defined local variable (static array of char), not a preprocessor macro.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists the predefined macros for compilation state and corrects that __func__ is not a macro.

probes: What goes wrong with function-like macros, and how do include guards differ from #pragma once?

hints.1: Macros are text replacement—think precedence, repeated arguments, and headers included twice.
hints.2: Cover parentheses, side-effect re-evaluation, #if family, guards vs #pragma once, then # and ##.
hints.3: No parens → precedence bugs; side effects re-evaluated; guards/#pragma once once-only; # stringises, ## pastes; __func__ is not a macro.

phases.goal: Contrast preprocessor macros with modern type-safe language features and include-guard styles.

must_hit.point: Modern C++ discourages macros for almost everything except #include and conditional compilation because the preprocessor is outside the type system and ignores namespaces and scope.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States macros lack type safety/scope/namespaces and should be limited to include and conditional compilation.

must_hit.point: Prefer const/constexpr variables over #define constants, inline functions and templates over function-like macros, and enum/enum class over #define flags.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Maps each modern feature to the macro use it replaces, citing type checking, single evaluation, and debugability.

must_hit.point: Include guards are portable conditional-compilation patterns; #pragma once is a widely supported single-line alternative that achieves the same once-only inclusion.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Notes most modern compilers support #pragma once as a one-line equivalent to the guard pattern.

probes: When would you still use the preprocessor, and what should replace #define constants and function-like macros?

hints.1: Ask what macros cannot see that the language can (types, scope, namespaces).
hints.2: Separate still-OK uses (#include, conditionals) from replacements (constexpr, inline/templates, enum).
hints.3: Keep macros for include/conditionals; use constexpr, inline/templates, and enum/enum class instead of #define constants, function macros, and flags.

phases.goal: Apply preprocessor knowledge to ODR/include-guard questions and justify preferring language features over macros.

must_hit.point: Include guards prevent violating the One Definition Rule (ODR) by stopping a header's contents (e.g. class definitions) from being pasted multiple times into the same compilation unit.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Answers 'What do include guards prevent?' with ODR / multiple definition of the same class in one translation unit.

must_hit.point: Prefer constexpr or inline over macros because macros lack type safety, ignore scope/namespaces, are hard to debug (debugger sees substituted text), and function-like macros risk double-evaluation.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists type safety, scope/namespaces, debug difficulty, and double-evaluation as reasons to prefer constexpr/inline.

must_hit.point: Macros have no type safety, so incompatible arguments can yield obscure compile errors or unexpected logic.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions absence of type checking as a distinct pitfall alongside precedence and re-evaluation.

probes: What do include guards prevent, and why prefer constexpr or inline over macros?

hints.1: Connect repeated #include of the same header to definitions appearing more than once.
hints.2: Name ODR for guards; for macros vs constexpr/inline, list type safety, scope, debugging, and evaluation count.
hints.3: Guards stop ODR violations from multi-pasted headers; constexpr/inline win on types, scope/namespaces, debug, and single evaluation.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Both stop a header from being processed more than once in a compilation unit. Guards use portable #ifndef/#define/#endif; #pragma once is a single-line form supported by most modern compilers with the same once-only effect.

tradeoffs.topic: #define macros vs const/constexpr, inline/templates, and enum
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Macros are untyped text outside namespaces/scope and can double-evaluate arguments. Prefer constexpr (or const) for constants, inline functions/templates for function-like macros (single evaluation, type-checked, debuggable), and enum/enum class for related named integer constants; keep macros mainly for #include and conditional compilation.

gotchas.trap: A function-like macro without parentheses around parameters and the whole body causes catastrophic operator-precedence bugs (e.g. BAD_SQ(i+1) expanding like 5+1*5+1).
gotchas.correction: Wrap every parameter and the entire macro body in parentheses, e.g. #define SQ(x) ((x)*(x)).

gotchas.trap: Passing arguments with side effects (like i++) into a macro causes double-evaluation bugs and can lead to undefined behaviour.
gotchas.correction: Avoid side-effect arguments in macros; prefer inline functions or templates that evaluate each argument once.

gotchas.trap: Treating __func__ as a preprocessor macro like __FILE__ or __LINE__.
gotchas.correction: __func__ is a compiler-provided implicitly defined local variable (a static array of char), not a preprocessor macro.

gotchas.trap: Relying on macros for constants, function-like helpers, or flags in modern C++.
gotchas.correction: Use constexpr/const, inline functions/templates, and enum/enum class instead; reserve the preprocessor mainly for #include and conditional compilation.
